grades.expert_take: At 6'4" and ~200 lb geared he needs the right shock spring and correct sag first; seat-bounce bottoming is spring/preload/HSC, square-edge harshness is too much LSC. Back LSC off from max, add HSC a quarter turn at a time, and confirm the spring rate. A revalve with a heavier spring is likely.
grades.note: Right call not to add HSC and good to flag the maxed LSC, but it stops short of telling him to back LSC off toward 15 out and test; ends on a question about the spring he already said he changed.

grades.expert_take: Check sag (104-106) and fork height and balance the front for a 150 lb rider on stock springs. More clamp offset reduces trail and quickens steering, so 24 mm clamps (stock 22) would likely make twitch and wobble worse; a steering stabilizer helps the wobble.
grades.note: Correctly notes more offset reduces trail and catches the 170 vs 150 lb mismatch, but 'hold off' plus a mechanical checklist gives no setup direction for twitch/tuck on a light rider with stock springs.

grades.expert_take: 91 mm sag with the collar fully loose means the spring is too stiff for him or the measurement is wrong. Check free sag, measure correctly (rider centered, in gear) and check for binding; a softer spring may be needed.
grades.note: Spots the air-fork/.44 spring mismatch, converts 4.3 kg/mm to about 42 N/mm and matches it to KTM's 143-165 lb band, then nails the real cause: sitting forward and measuring method.

grades.expert_take: The YZ250F's stock springs suit roughly 160-175 lb; at 158 lb, C-class, stock springs and valving are fine. Set race sag and check static sag, and tune clickers before thinking about a revalve.
grades.note: Clear keep-stock pick, cites Yamaha 4.7 N/mm and 56 N/mm, and catches the kg/mm vs N/mm unit mix-up in the rider's 5.4 figure.

grades.expert_take: For a 175 lb vet on natural terrain, .46 is close and he has already gone soft. With compression fully out, the remaining issue is valving, not springs, so a comfort revalve beats .44s. Lower oil only reduces bottoming resistance.
grades.note: Sensible pick (skip the .44s, spend on a revalve) with a good point that lower oil only affects late stroke; no published RM-Z250 numbers used and a little wordy.

grades.expert_take: Stock XACT air is about 155 psi; 140 is already low and he can go a little lower in 3-5 psi steps, but not bottoming isn't the goal. Bleed the outer legs, check break-in and seal friction, and account for front/rear balance after the stiffer rear spring.
grades.note: Gives the 155 psi stock figure, catches the clicker-direction ambiguity, bleed first, then a small 137 psi test with go-back conditions; asking for gear weight is fair since none was saved.

grades.expert_take: 162-164 psi is high for the AER48. For sand plowing vs braking-bump harshness, add rear sag (100-105) to unload the front, come down a little on air, keep some compression for support, and quicken rebound if it packs.
grades.note: Correctly reads 98 mm sag as rear-high/front-loaded, restores compression and tests 103-105 mm sag before small air and rebound steps; a pro would say this, but it is long.

grades.expert_take: The KTM AER chart is weight-graded; at 210-215 lb geared start in the upper part of the range (~162-168 psi), then adjust in 2-3 psi steps by sag and bottoming. The rear likely needs a stiffer spring.
grades.note: Picks the bottom of the 155-170 range for a 210-215 lb geared rider and argues weight does not justify more air, which runs against KTM's weight-graded AER pressure tables; the test-and-step method is fine.
numbers_to_verify: KTM 2018 250 SX-F AER manual pressure for an 85-95+ kg rider: I expect about 11.0-11.5 bar (160-167 psi), so a 160-165 psi start, not 155

grades.expert_take: For a trail race on stock MX valving, soften a bit: fork comp 2-3 clicks out, rebound 1-2 out, shock LSC 2-3 out and HSC 1/4 turn out, sag 105-108, keep fork height for stability.
grades.note: Sensible no-test plan: one fork compression change from the pits, then ordered shock HSC/LSC steps only if needed, with the correct warning not to slow rebound for woods.

grades.expert_take: Stock KX450 springs suit ~165-175 lb; at 200 geared he's slightly heavy, but near-endos after 10 years off are mostly technique (body position, chopping throttle on the face). Set sag, reset clickers to stock, then evaluate.
grades.note: Good returning-rider coaching and the right diagnostic question (braking dive vs kick off the face), plus Kawasaki baseline clickers; it doesn't set sag or give a first adjustment.

grades.expert_take: Common causes: oil level too high, trapped outer-chamber air, seal and bushing friction, or compression set too stiff. Check oil level against spec, bleed the outer legs, and confirm the model for the exact oil quantity.
grades.note: Correct that overfill shows as deep-stroke ramp-up, not initial stiffness, and that 130 psi may be too little; bleed step is right; no model, so no oil spec is acceptable.

grades.expert_take: Give Honda's stock clicker settings, but a 375 lb rider needs much stiffer custom springs and a revalve; stock settings are not usable. Strongly recommend a suspension shop.
grades.note: Gives Honda's standard clickers and says springs come first at 375 lb, but it should say outright that stock and even the optional stiff springs are far too soft and a custom spring/valve job is needed, not ask for sag first.

grades.expert_take: At 183 lb on the AER, 133 psi is low and many run 140-150. Harshness with 2 in. left may be the fork riding deep, slow rebound, or trapped air. Lowering oil won't fix harshness; bleed the outer legs, check alignment, consider valving.
grades.note: Answers the real-world psi question (about 140), says leave oil height alone and bleed the outer chambers; a mechanic might also suggest trying a few psi more, since riding deep can feel harsh.
numbers_to_verify: Tester report of about 10 psi gain on hot days with the AER fork (no cited fact)

grades.expert_take: The 2025 CRF450R has widely reported stiff, spiky chassis feel. Check engine-mount bolt torque, fork alignment and tire pressure; aftermarket engine mounts or a softer valving package are the usual fixes. It's a chassis trait more than an adjustment problem.
grades.note: Reasonable inspection checklist and answers the frame question, but it treats a widely reported 2025 CRF450R chassis harshness generically and offers no setup or parts direction.
numbers_to_verify: Handlebar-clamp recall said to cover the 2025 CRF450R: needs checking against Honda/NHTSA

grades.expert_take: The stiffer shock spring raises the rear and puts more load on the fork, making it feel harsher. Recheck sag (and free sag) with the new spring, go back to his old working fork settings, and balance by more sag or fork height instead of softening the fork further.
grades.note: Good diagnosis that the firmer rear shifts load to the fork and that dropping to 130 psi/fully open comp likely made it ride deep; going back to 135/22 is sensible, though more sag or fork height as a balance fix is missing.

grades.expert_take: Stock YZ250F springs suit ~165-175 lb; at 220 geared he needs stiffer springs at both ends. A respring doesn't always need a revalve: springs first, set sag, tune clickers.
grades.note: Correctly says a respring doesn't automatically need a revalve and that the fork likely needs stiffer springs; hedges on the shock for a 220 lb geared rider when stock is clearly light.

grades.expert_take: At 5 ft and 161 lb the stock springs are about right; lower the bike via fork height, sag or a linkage. Changing oil properly needs the legs out (or at least the caps off); 5 ml makes a small difference, deep in the stroke only.
grades.note: Answers directly (pull the legs), gives Honda's 380 cc standard and 5 cc steps, and correctly says less oil only softens deep in the travel; also a good point about bar reach for a 5 ft rider.

grades.expert_take: Someone set it very firm (heavy or fast rider, or whoops/sand). For a novice, go back to stock: fork comp 13, reb 10, LSC 7, shock reb 17. Expect a much plusher ride; the firm settings would feel harsh and kick.
grades.note: Clear table against Kawasaki's standards with the correct effect of each change, plausible reasons someone set it that way, and a sensible first reset step for a novice.

grades.expert_take: Getting to the KX shock rings usually means removing the subframe/airbox or muffler, or using a punch on the ring through the gap. Set race sag around 100-105 mm and check static sag.
grades.note: Practical answer (pull the rear frame/airbox, use hook spanners), clear sag steps, and the Kawasaki preload-ring range; long but all useful.

grades.expert_take: At 204 lb dry, a 5.0 shock spring on a KTM is about right and 105 mm sag with little preload is fine. Slap-down landings and bar beating point to fork valving, spring rate or new-cartridge break-in, not being oversprung.
grades.note: Doesn't answer whether he is oversprung; at 220 geared on a KTM a 5.0 shock spring is about right, and asking what units '5.0' is in adds nothing since kg/mm and N/mm are nearly the same here. Pointing him to the SFF converter's baseline is the useful part.

grades.expert_take: Stock YZ450F springs suit ~175-185 lb; a 230 lb slow vet will want stiffer springs (fork ~5.2+, shock ~60 N/mm). Springs first and set sag; revalve only if needed.
grades.note: Right order (springs first, valving only if needed) with Yamaha's 5.0 N/mm and 56 N/mm cited; at 230 lb it could say more plainly that both ends need heavier springs.

grades.expert_take: Give the Yamaha manual baseline for the 2006 YZ125 (note the 2020 build vs '06 mismatch) and sag about 95-100 mm.
grades.note: Labels a generic table as general guidance instead of giving the 2006 YZ125's own manual settings; the uniform 12/12/12/12 clickers look invented.
numbers_to_verify: 2006 YZ125 manual standard clickers (fork comp/reb, shock LSC/HSC/reb) and sag: should come from the Yamaha manual, not a generic table

grades.expert_take: Bar swapping at speed on hardpack: check sag and fork height, look for the front riding too low or the rear too high, rebound balance, tire pressure and head bearings, and fit a steering stabilizer.
grades.note: Mechanical checks and the accel-vs-braking question are fine, but he asked what to do and gets no setup direction (sag, fork height, rebound balance, steering damper) for headshake at speed on hardpack.

grades.expert_take: Learn sag (free and rider, 105 target), reset clickers and air to stock for his weight, then change one thing at a time. Don't spend $1,500 yet.
grades.note: Exactly what a fast beginner needs: don't spend $1,500 yet, step-by-step sag, then reset to Husqvarna's baseline and change one thing at a time.
numbers_to_verify: 2020 FC 250 fork air 10.4 bar (151 psi) and 40-hour suspension service interval are not in cited_facts

grades.expert_take: Rear kick: wrong rebound (too fast, or packing), wrong sag or spring, or too much HSC. Set sag, start from stock, test rebound a few clicks at a time before buying a shock.
grades.note: Keeps the stock shock, gives KTM's baseline, checks chain and linkage, and correctly splits the kick into rebound-too-fast vs packing vs compression cases.

grades.expert_take: At 5,700-8,000 ft, lean it out: main 1-2 sizes smaller, needle clip up one, possibly a smaller pilot, adjust the air screw. Yamaha's manual has an altitude/temperature chart.
grades.note: Gives the stock jetting but won't give a leaner starting combination for 5,700-8,000 ft, which was the whole question; Yamaha's own altitude/temperature chart would have answered it.

grades.expert_take: Plug fouling on the 2025 TBI two-stroke: check for a crank seal leak (gearbox oil level dropping), fuel pressure and injector, plug cap; 50:1 is fine. Test the sensor rather than swapping parts.
grades.note: Right priorities: test the CCP sensor before replacing it, check fuel pressure and injector sealing, and ask about gearbox oil level as a crank seal check; notes the 1:60 and BR8ES spec.

grades.expert_take: Fouling on a 2025 TBI 125 SX: correct premix and plug, fresh fuel, check the fuel pump and injector; light riding makes it worse but isn't the whole cure.
grades.note: Gives KTM's 40:1 mix, BR10ECMVX plug and idle spec and a sound fouling diagnosis; the dealer fuel-pump report is properly hedged.

grades.expert_take: In the Power Tuner app all zeros means stock (no offset); load the zeroed map to revert.
grades.note: Correct and short: zeroed cells mean no correction (stock), load it to both map slots.

grades.expert_take: The Powerflow kit plus the lid off leans it out; the bog on a snap in neutral happens even on a stock 450. Use the Rideology app to add about 3-5% fuel in the low-rpm/low-throttle cells and test while riding.
grades.note: Rightly says snapping it open in neutral isn't a fair test, but he asked where and how much fuel to add after a Powerflow kit with the lid off, and gets no starting cells or percentages.

grades.expert_take: Rich bottom: drop the pilot one size, check float height. Running best at 2-3 turns on the air screw confirms the pilot is rich.
grades.note: Clear pick (a #48 first, after checking float height at Yamaha's 6.5 mm) and correctly reads the air screw position as a rich pilot circuit.

grades.expert_take: Colder, denser air means go richer: one main jet up, needle clip down one (richer), maybe the pilot up one. Roughly one main size per 15-20 F.
grades.note: Correct direction and size of step: one main richer for colder, denser air, and dropping the clip richens the midrange, with the right warnings.

grades.expert_take: A hanging idle that then dies is usually an air leak (crank seal, intake boot, reed gasket) or a pilot circuit problem. A crank seal can pass a pressure test and still leak under vacuum.
grades.note: Correctly points to the pilot circuit or an air leak, notes a crank seal can pass a pressure test and still leak under vacuum, and the choke test is a good diagnostic.

grades.expert_take: Intermittent cut-out: kill switch and wiring, ignition and stator connectors, ground, TPS connector, fuel pump/relay on the TBI 300 SX.
grades.note: Right safety call and the right order (connectors including the kill switch and TPS, tank vent, fuel), plus KTM's one-hour fuel screen service.

grades.expert_take: TBI TC250 that dies at idle: idle adjuster or dirty bypass, TPS calibration, fuel pump/injector, air leak; clean the throttle body and reset the ECU/TPS.
grades.note: Sensible focus on the idle adjuster, throttle return and the TPS baseline for a TBI that won't idle; somewhat generic beyond that.

grades.expert_take: Removing the backfire screen gains little; the ECU compensates only partly; it risks backfire damage. Charge the battery. Not worth it.
grades.note: Correct to refit the screen and that the ECU won't reliably compensate; the 2021 ECU update point is useful but not cited.

grades.expert_take: Give the 2022 YZ125 stock jetting; for a lean bog with the GYTR kit check float height, pilot/air screw and needle clip, and confirm the kit spec.
grades.note: Answers with the 2022 stock jetting specs and sensibly questions whether it is really lean, but gives no GYTR kit spec and ends on a three-part question.

grades.expert_take: Late-day popping and power loss that resets on restart is heat-related: fuel pump/filter, injector, sensor or ECU, stator; check the fan and coolant, vapor lock, tank vent.
grades.note: Correctly reads late-day failure that clears on restart as heat-related fuel or electrical, and asks for testing while the fault is present.

grades.expert_take: With an older Vortex you lose on-the-fly switching but can run one good map; it's a cost vs convenience trade, and most won't miss it if the map is right.
grades.note: Good pick, and it correctly notes the 2023+ switch also runs traction control, launch and quickshifter, not only maps.

grades.expert_take: The KTM Connectivity Unit (2023+) works with the KTMconnect app to change maps, traction control and quickshift, and uses GPS for lap and ride tracking. Give pros and cons.
grades.note: Vague; doesn't say what the KTM Connectivity Unit actually does (map, TC and quickshift settings, GPS lap timing) or how owners rate it.

grades.expert_take: A cap gauge reading 350 is suspect; at 18 h after the recall, recheck the valve cover gasket and plug seals and check the breather isn't blocked. Overheating raises pressure, so check coolant and airflow.
grades.note: Right safety call and the overfill check with Kawasaki's capacities; it could say plainly that a cap gauge reading is suspect and that idling or poor airflow is the usual cause.

grades.expert_take: Bikes normally ship with oil or the dealer fills it at setup. A big blue cloud on throttle on a new four-stroke means overfill/breather carryover or rings not sealing; check the oil level and the breather.
grades.note: Answers the oil question, says a blue cloud isn't break-in, lists overfill/breather, rings and valve seals in order, and sends it back under warranty.

grades.expert_take: Sudden vibration at 44 h: stop riding, check engine mount bolts, sprockets/chain, the balancer shaft/gear, cam chain; check the oil screen for metal.
grades.note: Correct: stop, check the oil and screens for metal, consider loose mounts or the balancer before blaming the oil pump.

grades.expert_take: A CRF boils on the stand quickly with no airflow, but under 5 minutes means check coolant level and air, the cap, head gasket and water pump. Don't idle it on the stand; more oil isn't the fix.
grades.note: Correct that more oil isn't the fix and that idling on a stand boils it; won't give 2019 figures but the checks are sound.

grades.expert_take: KTM's 15 h is a piston-replacement interval; many recreational riders go about 25-40 h depending on use. Inspect at 15 h before stretching it.
grades.note: Correct that 15 h is KTM's piston replacement interval, but it gives no real-world range for recreational riders, which is what he asked.

grades.expert_take: An empty radiator on a new bike may have caused overheating damage in a short run; check the head gasket and do a leak-down. The fast-idle knob for cold starts is normal.
grades.note: Right call to stop and get a dealer pressure test, with Honda's capacity and normal overflow figures cited correctly.

grades.expert_take: Known 2023-24 CRF250R checks: valve clearances (intake), clutch, airbox sealing; buy the one with records.
grades.note: Good buyer's checklist and a clear pick; the filter/airbox claim is uncited and valve wear could be stressed more.

grades.expert_take: A recurring weep-hole drip is a seal leak; after a cover replacement it points to the mechanical seal, shaft or bearing. Replace the seals and impeller shaft under warranty.
grades.note: Correct that a recurring weep-hole drip after a warranty cover is a seal or shaft problem, not cold shrinkage, with good tracing and warranty steps.

grades.expert_take: The hole under the water pump is the weep hole; oil from it means the pump-shaft oil seal. Overfill can make it worse. Check the level and the seal under warranty.
grades.note: Identifies the weep hole, says oil means the oil-side seal, gives Kawasaki's capacities, and sends it back to the dealer.

grades.expert_take: Spooge at the exhaust joint on a new two-stroke at 40:1 and low revs is normal; check the pipe springs and O-ring, clean it. Not harmful; ride it harder.
grades.note: Right: spooge at the pipe joint is common, 40:1 matches KTM, a small smear won't hurt it, and it says when it needs fixing.
